content: Congenital syphilis is a severe condition that results in fetal or perinatal death in approximately 40% of affected infants. This condition was first described in the 15th century and has long been recognized as a distinct syndrome caused by transmission from an infected adult. Various theories have been proposed to explain the transmission of syphilis, including paternal transmission and transmission through an infected wet nurse. However, transplacental transmission from an asymptomatic infected mother was first documented in 1906. Despite the availability of penicillin treatment for syphilis during pregnancy, congenital syphilis has not been eradicated. Since the 1970s, the incidence of congenital syphilis has closely mirrored the rates of primary and secondary syphilis in women. In 1986, the number of reported cases of congenital syphilis in the United States reached 365, the highest in 15 years, with nearly one in every 10,000 live-born infants affected. The proportion of stillbirths caused by syphilis remains unknown. In July 1987, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) convened a group of 10 consultants to address the problem of congenital syphilis and develop potential solutions. The resulting guidelines, published as a supplement to the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), aim to provide focused and coordinated guidance for healthcare providers. While some aspects of the guidelines are based on limited data, they represent the best judgment of experts in the field. Surveillance Surveillance of congenital syphilis should be conducted at local, state, and national levels. The provisional case definition includes any infant under 12 months of age with one of the following: 1. A reactive non-treponemal serologic test for syphilis confirmed by a reactive treponemal test. 2. A positive darkfield microscopic examination of a non-oral mucous membrane. 3. A positive fluorescent antibody test for Treponema pallidum on any lesion. Physicians, clinics, and hospitals are required to report all cases meeting the provisional definition to local public health authorities. Laboratories must also report indicative findings. Areas with five or more women diagnosed with early infectious syphilis per 100,000 population should establish active surveillance systems for congenital syphilis at key hospitals. Hospitals in high-incidence areas or those serving at-risk populations should routinely perform serologic tests for syphilis (STS) using umbilical cord blood samples. Confirmed or compatible cases, as well as those requiring additional information for classification, should be reported to state public health authorities. A Congenital Syphilis Follow-up Form (CDC 73.126) should be completed and forwarded through local and state public health authorities to the CDC for all infants, including stillbirths, who have not been classified as unlikely. Cases lost to follow-up should also be described in detail on the form. Surveillance data collected on these forms are used to determine the reasons for specific cases and to identify trends. All forms should be completed by the time an infant reaches eight months of age, including cases lost to follow-up. Stillbirths should also be evaluated for syphilis, and those consistent with congenital syphilis should be documented on the same form. Diagnostic Classifications of Congenital Syphilis A confirmed case of congenital syphilis is defined by the identification of Treponema pallidum through darkfield microscopy, fluorescent antibody testing, or other specific stains in specimens from lesions, autopsy material, placenta, or umbilical cord. Alternatively, a live-born infant with no symptoms whose mother was treated for syphilis during pregnancy and demonstrated a fourfold or greater fall in titer, with the infant's STS being fourfold or lower than the maternal titer at the time of treatment, may also be classified as a confirmed case. Control Controlling early infectious syphilis is critical to preventing congenital syphilis. When the prevalence of infectious syphilis increases among women of reproductive age, cases of congenital syphilis are likely to follow. Recent years have seen increased prevalence in several areas of the United States. To prevent future cases, sexually transmitted disease (STD) control programs must emphasize early syphilis control, particularly in high-incidence areas. Disease Intervention Activities for Early Infectious Syphilis Traditional tools for controlling early syphilis in the United States include interviewing patients to identify sexual partners, rapid partner notification, selective re-interviews, and clustering around the patient and their examined partners to identify others at risk. Recommended techniques and procedures are discussed in disease intervention courses sponsored by the Division of Sexually Transmitted Diseases. The pregnancy status of women diagnosed with syphilis and the partners of men with syphilis should be assessed. Women in high-incidence neighborhoods should be identified and referred for serologic testing and prenatal care. Educational messages should be delivered to the medical community about laboratory tests, diagnostic criteria, treatment, and follow-up for at-risk patients. Public service messages should target women who share demographic characteristics with those most often diagnosed with early syphilis, such as young, single, minority women living in central city neighborhoods. Prenatal Care Comprehensive prenatal care initiated early in pregnancy is essential for preventing congenital syphilis. However, financial barriers, limited availability of healthcare providers, communication difficulties, and organizational issues often hinder access to care, particularly for poor and minority women. Modifications to the current system that reduce these obstacles would improve opportunities for women with syphilis to receive care. Laboratory Testing The diagnosis of syphilis relies on appropriate standard laboratory tests. The quality of these tests depends on the use of high-quality reagents and well-trained personnel. Laboratories must adhere to strict quality control procedures and participate in regular performance evaluations. Treatment in Pregnancy No major clinical trials have evaluated the currently recommended treatments for syphilis in pregnant patients in the past 20 years. While individual treatment failures have been reported, the lack of denominator data prevents accurate calculation of failure rates. Available data suggest that treatment efficacy varies with the stage of maternal infection and pregnancy. For example, treatment failure rates may be higher among women with secondary syphilis and those treated in the last trimester of pregnancy. Penicillin remains the treatment of choice for syphilis in pregnancy, even for penicillin-allergic patients, provided they undergo desensitization. Desensitization can be achieved through gradually increasing oral or intravenous doses over 3-4 hours until full tolerance is achieved. Intravenous desensitization allows for immediate cessation if an allergic reaction occurs but is associated with a higher frequency of reactions.
